text:
Apollo 13: The Long Way Home

On the evening of April 13, 1970, Apollo 13 was nearly 200,000 miles from Earth, and the people in Mission Control thought it was going well. Launch two days earlier had been mostly clean. The crew was on course for the Moon's Fra Mauro highlands: commander Jim Lovell, lunar module pilot Fred Haise and command module pilot Jack Swigert. Swigert had joined the crew three days before launch, after the original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, was exposed to German measles and grounded. The television networks had stopped carrying the astronauts' live broadcasts. Going to the Moon had started to look routine.

A few minutes after that evening's broadcast ended, Houston asked Swigert to do a routine job: turn on the fans that stirred the supercooled oxygen in the service module's tanks. Seconds later the crew heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder. Warning lights came on. Swigert radioed, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." When the ground asked him to repeat it, Lovell answered: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first nobody understood how bad it was. The instruments were confusing, and some controllers thought the sensors themselves had failed. Then Lovell looked out a window and saw a cloud of gas streaming away from the spacecraft into space. "We are venting something," he reported. It was oxygen. One of the two oxygen tanks had blown up, and the blast had damaged the other one, which was now leaking.

The oxygen did two jobs. The crew breathed it, and it also fed the three fuel cells that made the command module's electricity and water. As the pressure fell, the fuel cells died one after another. The command module, Odyssey, was the only part of the spacecraft with a heat shield, so it was the only part that could bring the crew home. Its power was going, and its batteries had to be saved for the last hours of the flight and the fall through the atmosphere.

There was one way out. The lunar module, Aquarius, was docked to Odyssey's nose. It was built to keep two men alive for about two days on the Moon's surface. Now it would have to carry three men for about four days. Within about an hour of the explosion, Lovell and Haise were in Aquarius bringing its systems up, and Swigert was shutting Odyssey down one switch at a time. He copied its guidance alignment over by hand so the navigation reference would not be lost. When he finished, the command module was cold and dark. The lunar module had become a lifeboat.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and the controllers working with him had to answer a hard question: how to get the crew home. The fastest option was to fire the big service module engine, turn the spacecraft around and head straight back. Nobody knew how badly the explosion had damaged that engine, and an engine failure would kill the crew. They chose to keep going. Apollo 13 would swing around the far side of the Moon and let lunar gravity send it back toward Earth.

That plan had its own problem. Earlier in the flight the spacecraft had left its "free-return" path, the course that would have brought it home with no further engine burns. To get back on that path, the crew fired the lunar module's descent engine, which had been designed to land on the Moon, not to steer a stack of two linked spacecraft. The burn worked. Late on April 14, Houston time, Apollo 13 passed behind the Moon and out of radio contact. On that pass it went farther from Earth than any people had gone before or have gone since. About two hours later the crew made a second, longer descent engine burn to speed up and cut roughly ten hours off the trip home. They had very little margin, so every hour saved counted.

Getting the trajectory right only solved part of the problem, because keeping three men alive inside Aquarius for four days raised its own. Power came first. To make the lunar module's batteries last, the crew turned off nearly everything, including the heaters. Temperatures inside fell close to freezing. Frost formed on the windows, and the men had trouble sleeping in the cold. Water was the next shortage. The crew cut back to a small fraction of their normal intake, partly to save water for cooling the equipment. All three became dehydrated, and Haise developed a urinary tract infection that gave him a fever by the end of the flight.

Carbon dioxide was the most dangerous of these problems. Every breath the astronauts let out added to it, and the cabin depended on canisters of lithium hydroxide to absorb it. Aquarius had enough canisters for two men for a short stay on the Moon. Odyssey had plenty of spares, but they were square, and the sockets in the lunar module took round ones. Carbon dioxide levels started to climb toward the point where they would cause headaches, confusion and eventually death.

Engineers on the ground worked out an adapter using only things the crew had on board: plastic bags, cardboard from the flight plan covers, hoses from the spacesuits and plenty of gray duct tape. Then they read the instructions up to the spacecraft step by step. Lovell and his crew built it, connected it, and watched the carbon dioxide readings drop. It is one of the best-known improvised repairs in the history of engineering, and it worked because people on the ground had first built and tested the same thing out of the same materials.

The trajectory still needed adjusting. With the guidance computer switched off to save power, the crew made one course correction by sight. Lovell kept the edge of the Earth, the line between day and night, steady in his window while the engine fired for about fourteen seconds. Haise and Swigert called out times and helped keep the spacecraft pointed. That burn was enough to keep the spacecraft inside the narrow corridor it had to hit on reentry. If it came in too steeply it would burn up, and if it came in too shallowly it would skip off the atmosphere.

The last challenge was bringing Odyssey back to life. No one had ever powered up a command module that had sat cold and dark for days in space, and the batteries held barely enough power to do it. On the ground, Mattingly, the astronaut who had been bumped from the flight, spent long hours in the simulator with other engineers working out a power-up sequence that stayed within that budget. The crew used some of Aquarius's power to recharge Odyssey's batteries, then followed the new checklist.

On April 17 the crew separated from the service module. As it drifted away they saw the damage for the first time: an entire panel had been blown off the side. They photographed it, unsure whether the explosion had also cracked the heat shield next to it. A few hours later they let Aquarius go, and Mission Control thanked the lunar module for its service.

Every reentry included a few minutes of radio blackout, when the superheated air around the capsule blocked radio signals. This one lasted longer than usual. For about six minutes no one on the ground knew whether the heat shield had held. Then Swigert's voice came through. Shortly after noon Houston time, Odyssey splashed down under its parachutes in the South Pacific near Samoa, and the USS Iwo Jima picked up the crew. They were thin, exhausted and cold, and they were alive.

An investigation found that the problem started years before launch. A thermostatic switch inside the oxygen tank had never been upgraded to match a change in the spacecraft's power supply. During ground testing the switch welded shut while the tank was being emptied with its heater on, and temperatures inside rose high enough to damage the wire insulation. When Swigert turned on the fans in flight, the bare wires sparked and the tank exploded. NASA redesigned the tanks, and Apollo flew four more missions to the Moon.

Apollo 13 never landed, but people often call it a "successful failure." That is because hundreds of people on the ground and three men in space solved, one after another, problems that nobody had planned for, and they did it in time.
